title: Patience, again
hook: patience in obedience, patience from sin, patience in trials

segments.voice: Yesterday, zuhd, detachment, and your line: not owned by it. Did the thing you found actually leave the house, and how long did the tug last? Day one thousand two hundred seventy-four.

Three people, same morning. The first is getting out of a warm bed in the dark for the dawn prayer, and every part of her wants to stay. The second is scrolling, and a message arrives he knows he shouldn't answer the way he wants to. The third is in a hospital corridor, waiting for a door to open with news. Three very different mornings. Teachers of the inward path would give all three the same name. Patience. Not one patience, they say, but three. Today, the station we've met before, opened up.
screen: `OUT OF A WARM BED.` → `A MESSAGE NOT TO ANSWER.` → `A HOSPITAL CORRIDOR.`

segments.voice: In Arabic, patience is sabr. In Pickthall's translation, the Qur'an says: "O ye who believe! Seek help in steadfastness and prayer. Lo! Allah is with the steadfast." Pickthall says steadfastness, and that's a good clue. Sabr isn't sitting still. It's holding steady. Scholars of the inward path describe three kinds. Patience in obedience: keeping on with a good thing when it's hard, the woman getting out of bed. Patience from sin: holding back from a wrong thing when it's tempting, the man not hitting send. And patience in trials: staying steady when something hits you that you didn't choose, the person in the corridor. A person can be strong in one and thin in another. Somebody who never misses a prayer can still fire off the angry message. Somebody calm in a crisis can still struggle with the alarm clock. Then there's a moment in Sahih al-Bukhari. The Prophet ﷺ passes a woman weeping at a grave and tells her to be patient. She doesn't recognize him and snaps back that he hasn't been struck by what she has. Later she learns who it was, and comes to his door to explain. He doesn't scold her. He says, in effect, that patience is at the first blow. Not the weeping. The first moment. This whole week has been stations like this one: good character, al-Ghazali's Revival, turning back, watchfulness, the evening ledger, detachment, and now patience. Each one, it turns out, needs this one to last.
screen: `SABR: HOLDING STEADY.` · `IN OBEDIENCE, FROM SIN, IN TRIALS.` · `PATIENCE IS AT THE FIRST BLOW.` · `A WEEK OF STATIONS.`

segments.voice: The practice: pick one patience. Settle, and breathe. Hold up the three, one at a time. Keeping on with a good thing. Holding back from a wrong one. Staying steady in something hard. Ask which one is thinnest in your life right now. Don't pick the one you're already good at. When you have it, find one place today where it will be tested. The alarm. The reply. The waiting room. Picture the first moment of that test, the first blow, and picture yourself holding steady for just that moment. If you pray, you can rest on the line: Allah is with the steadfast. The bell holds the time.
Patience. Sabr: holding steady, in doing good, in holding back from wrong, and in what life brings. Today's word.
Your line: three patiences. Today, watch for the one you chose, and when it comes, give it the first moment. Just the first. Tomorrow, gratitude, again. Day one thousand two hundred seventy-four.

howItsDone: Muslims speak of sabr in three kinds: in keeping up acts of worship, in holding back from wrongdoing, and in bearing hardship; people often remind one another to have sabr in times of loss.
